newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Uzbek forces join battlefront, raise Afghan stakes.
newsitem.headline: Uzbek forces join battlefront, raise Afghan stakes.

text.p: The forces of powerful Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum rolled onto the front line of Afghanistan's latest battle for power on Thursday, dramatically escalating a war between the Taleban militia and the government it ousted.
But even as a dozen Uzbek tanks and hundreds of men poured out of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains, Dostum and the purist Islamic Taleban were still talking peace.

Afghan-watchers regard Dostum as heading perhaps the most powerful single fighting force in Afghanistan that could influence the fate of Kabul, seized three weeks ago by Taleban Islamic fighters who control two-thirds of the country.

The Taleban on Wednesday rejected an ultimatum from the ousted government's military chief to quit Kabul or face bloodshed, saying there were enough Taleban to defend the city on which they have imposed Islam's stern Sharia law.
But they might not be able to hold it against both Dostum and the forces of ex-defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood, whose spokesman billed Dostum's deployment as a victory.

Peace calls came from India and Iran and the world's largest Moslem organisation, the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC), grouping more than 50 Moslem countries. Japan offered to host any peace talks.
Pakistan said President Farooq Leghari, keen to allay Central Asian fears about the rise of the radical Taleban militia, will fly to the Uzbek capital Tashkent on Friday.

Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters in Kabul the Taleban were satisfied with Pakistani-brokered talks in Dostum's northern stronghold on Wednesday and that the Uzbek leader has assured them he would not join the battle.

"Deployment and talks are not necessarily inconsistent. Dostum is clearly making himself the key to a deal and his deployment just strengthens the pressure on the Taleban." said one veteran Afghan watcher in Kabul.
"Even if the Uzbeks join the battle, the hope of successful talks is not dead."

Nevertheless, fears mounted in Kabul of yet another battle for a city that bears the massive scars of factional power struggles in the past four years after escaping largely unscathed Afghanistan's previous 13 years of war.
Masood said he left Kabul without a battle on September 27 as the Taleban descended on it to spare the city another bloodbath. Now he has told the Taleban to quit or face a fight.
The Taleban authorities waved off the threat, saying they had enough fighters to defend the capital.
The Uzbek soldiers, who live under a liberal Islamic regime and despise the Taleban's imposition of strict Sharia law wherever they have taken control, seemed eager for a fight.
"We came from Salang and we're going to Kabul. We're going to bash the Taleban today. There are 5,000 of us coming," one said as he headed for the front.

The Uzbeks deployed alongside the forces of Masood, who has pushed back the Taleban from the Salang, out of the town of Charikar a 30-minute drive south, and attacked their main air base at Bagram in the past week.
They immediately came under Taleban shell fire as they moved onto high ground between Charikar and the junction just south of the town which leads to Bagram another five km (three miles) to the east.

Masood's forces, who have been pushed back over the past two days, and the Taleban traded heavy fire all day in the battle for control of the junction of the two roads leading to Kabul some 50 km (30 miles) away.

Witnesses said there appeared to have been little movement on the ground by either side during the day and Masood still had not taken Bagram, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul despite days of fighting over it.
The Taleban have poured hundreds of reinforcements and air power into the battle, one bomb landing just five metres (yards) from the highway on Thursday.
Dr Abdul Rawuz said his Charikar hosital needed help desperately. "Any wounded person who comes here now will surely die because we have not even one medicine," he said.
The Taleban have suffered several hundred casualties in the fighting north of Kabul in the past two weeks. It is not known how many men Masood has lost.
Hundreds of people have fled their villages on the sun-baked plain where the battle is raging, some heading for Kabul carrying what little they can and others to the north.
